title: I Haven't Got Time
author: Cline, Paul
summary: Paul Cline uses three composite classroom scenarios, a teacher introducing a new concept, a teacher modelling a writing style, and a teacher returning assessment feedback, each observed by an instructional coach, to argue that "I haven't got time" is usually the wrong response to good coaching suggestions, because skipping a technique to save time in the moment tends to cost more time later. In each scenario, he first shows the coach's hypothesis-driven suggestion, more retrieval practice, an extended "We" phase of modelling, having students apply feedback rather than just record it, and the teacher's likely time-pressured objection, then replays the same lesson showing what actually happens when the suggestion is skipped: confused re-explanation, repeated individual correction of the same mistake, and students who can state their target but can't demonstrate what it looks like. His argument culminates in a simple reframe: investing time in prior-knowledge activation, extended co-construction, and applied feedback is "slowing down to speed up," trading a small upfront time cost for a larger downstream saving in re-teaching and re-explaining. He closes by connecting to a companion post on routinising the mechanics of a lesson, framing efficient routines as the precondition that frees up time for teachers to actually invest in these techniques.
points: Cline's structural device, showing the same lesson twice, once with a technique skipped and once with it included, makes the "cost of skipping" concrete rather than asserted.

His three techniques, retrieval practice, extended modelling, and feedback application, are each shown producing a specific downstream time cost when skipped: repeated re-explanation, repeated individual correction, and unchanged future mistakes.
He explicitly credits an instructional coach observing through a hypothesis-based feedback approach as the analytic lens driving each scenario's diagnosis.
His closing move ties the argument to a companion post by Jo Castelino, positioning routinised lesson mechanics and time-investing pedagogy as two halves of the same solution to "not enough time."
quotes: The more I’ve really unpacked what effective teaching looks like, the more I’ve come to realise that to do it really properly takes more time than I have available.

Tim’s coach wonders if students will struggle to understand the new concept because they don’t see how it fits with what they already know. Would they have benefited from some retrieval practice based around prior, prerequisite knowledge in order to ‘warm them up’ and make them more receptive to the new information?

In Tim’s lesson, students are struggling to get to grips with the new idea. It doesn’t really make sense to them and when Tim asks them to explain it they can’t do much more than repeat back some of the words with lost expressions and helpless shrugs.
Sometimes you need to slow down to speed up. Investing the time to get things right at the outset means smoother progress later on.

We can’t create more time. It might be possible for school leaders to think creatively and flexibly about things like the curriculum, timetabling, staffing and come up with solutions that give us a little more. But these things don’t happen quickly or often.
